opus-5.5.text:
I think navigation played a really foundational role, maybe more than people realize today. If you look back at the history of embodied AI as a research field, navigation was the first task where we could really close the loop between perception, decision-making, and action in a way that scaled.

Around 2017 to 2019, with simulators like Habitat, AI2-THOR, and Gibson, the community suddenly had environments where an agent could move through realistic 3D scenes, see from a first-person view, and be trained and evaluated at massive scale. Tasks like point-goal navigation, object-goal navigation, and later vision-and-language navigation gave us a shared benchmark culture. That is very important for a field. It defined what "embodied" meant: the agent is situated, it perceives egocentrically, and its actions change what it sees next.

Navigation also taught us some key lessons that shaped the mainstream direction. One is that end-to-end learning with large-scale simulation data can work surprisingly well. Point-goal navigation got close to "solved" in simulation with billions of frames of reinforcement learning. That gave people confidence in the sim-to-real, data-driven paradigm. Another lesson is the importance of semantics and language. Once you move from "go to coordinates" to "go find the chair" or "follow these instructions," you naturally need vision-language understanding, which bridged embodied AI with the progress in large models.

But I would also say navigation showed us its own limits. Navigation is, in a sense, a relatively low-dimensional action problem. You move a base around; you don't really change the world. The hard part of embodied intelligence, the part that creates real value, is interaction: manipulation, contact, handling deformable or articulated objects, using tools. That's where the physics gets complicated, the data is far scarcer, and simulation is much harder to get right.

So my view is that navigation established the framework, the benchmarks, the simulation-driven methodology, and the combination with language models. Now the mainstream direction has shifted toward mobile manipulation and dexterous manipulation, where navigation becomes a component, a capability the robot must have, but not the end goal. Today we talk about vision-language-action models and generalist robot policies, and I see navigation as the stepping stone that made that conversation possible. It proved embodied learning could scale, and then the field moved on to the harder question of how robots can actually do things in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says navigation agents perceive egocentrically and that their actions change what they see next, conveying that movement changes the view and calls for ongoing perception.

r002.rationale: It describes navigation as closing the loop between perception, decision-making, and action, but does not say researchers pursued this approach even for tasks solvable with traditional modular methods.

r003.rationale: It says the field shifted toward manipulation and that navigation became one component, but does not identify closed-loop manipulation research as an extension of navigation’s perception-action approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think of navigation as the first capability that forced embodied intelligence to confront the real world, and that is why it ended up defining the mainstream direction.

Before navigation became a research focus, a lot of "embodied" work was really perception in disguise. You detect objects, you segment scenes, but the agent never has to act on what it sees. Navigation changed that. Suddenly the model has to make a decision, move, observe the consequence, and update. That closed loop between perception and action is the essence of embodiment, and navigation is the simplest task that demands it.

The second thing navigation did was push the field toward learning in simulation at scale. Habitat, AI2-THOR, Gibson, Matterport3D, all of these emerged because navigation needed thousands of environments and millions of trajectories. That infrastructure, and the sim-to-real question it raised, became shared infrastructure for everything that followed, including manipulation.

Third, navigation set the template for how language enters embodiment. Vision-language navigation, where you follow an instruction like "go past the kitchen and stop at the second door," was one of the earliest places where grounding language in physical action was studied seriously. When people now talk about vision-language-action models, that lineage goes straight back through VLN.

I would also say navigation clarified what "general" should mean. Early systems were trained per environment. The shift to zero-shot navigation in unseen buildings, and later to open-vocabulary goals like "find me a coffee cup," taught the community that generalization across environments and across semantic goals is the real benchmark, not performance in one map.

So I don't think navigation is the whole of embodied intelligence. Manipulation is harder and arguably more valuable economically. But navigation was the proving ground. It established the loop, the data pipeline, the language interface, and the standard for generalization. Those four things are what the mainstream direction is built on today.

r002.rationale: It describes navigation as a closed-loop task, but does not state that researchers pursued this approach even for tasks solvable with traditional modular methods.

r003.rationale: It says navigation infrastructure later served manipulation, but does not identify closed-loop manipulation as an extension of navigation’s perception-action approach.

astra-6.text:
I think navigation helped establish a basic paradigm for embodied intelligence: an agent has to perceive its surroundings, decide what to do, act, and then adjust based on what actually happens. It’s a closed loop. You can’t judge intelligence only by whether the system gives a good answer; you have to ask whether it can accomplish something in an environment.

Navigation makes that very concrete. If I ask a robot to go to another room and find a chair, it needs to connect language with visual perception, understand spatial relationships, plan a route, and deal with uncertainty along the way. Those capabilities have to work together, so navigation became a natural starting point for studying embodied intelligence as a complete system.

But I’d distinguish being foundational from being sufficient. Moving through the world is only part of the problem. Manipulation adds another layer: the robot has to make contact with objects and change their state. So I see navigation as helping establish the methods and the research direction, while the broader goal is to bring movement, perception, and interaction together.

r001.rationale: The response describes navigation as a perception–action loop but does not explain that movement changes the agent’s view of its environment.

r002.rationale: It does not say researchers pursued closed-loop perception and action for tasks that traditional modular methods could solve.

r003.rationale: It presents manipulation as adding contact and object-state changes, but does not identify closed-loop manipulation research as an extension of navigation’s perception–action approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think navigation is one of the foundational capabilities of embodied intelligence. An agent has to understand where it is, where it wants to go, and how to get there while interacting with a changing environment. That brings perception, spatial understanding, planning, and action into a single problem.

What makes navigation especially valuable is that it closes the loop. A system cannot just produce a plausible answer; it has to act, observe what happened, and adjust. If an obstacle appears or its understanding of the environment is wrong, it needs to recover.

But I wouldn’t equate navigation with embodied intelligence as a whole. Reaching a table is different from picking up a cup and using it. Navigation provides an important foundation, while manipulation and more complex interactions expand what the agent can actually accomplish. Its role in shaping the mainstream direction is to push us toward systems that connect understanding with action and can demonstrate that connection in the physical world.

r002.rationale: It describes closed-loop behavior, but does not say researchers pursued it even for tasks solvable with traditional modular methods.

r003.rationale: It presents manipulation as extending what agents can do, but does not identify closed-loop manipulation research as an extension of navigation’s perception-action approach.
